summary: Defines a mobility option that lets Mobile IPv6 nodes identify themselves using something other than their home address, such as an NAI, an FQDN, an IMSI, or an MSISDN. It can be used in messages carrying a mobility header. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: A moving device can introduce itself with a name tag other than its address, like a phone number or username, when it talks to its home base.

questions: what is the mobile node identifier option
what is mn-nai in mobile ipv6
how does mobile ipv6 identify a node by nai
subtitle: A Mobile IPv6 option that lets a mobile node identify itself with a name such as a user@realm NAI instead of only its home address.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 identifies mobility entities only by an IPv6 address, but deployments also need to identify a mobile node by other identifiers such as an NAI or an IMSI.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Mobile Node Identifier option for the Mobility header. A Subtype field says what kind of identifier follows, and subtype 1 is the MN-NAI, written as user@realm.
tldr.outcome: A node can now be identified for things like AAA-based authentication or dynamic home address allocation. The cost is a privacy risk, because a stable identifier can be used to track a user.

today: RFC 4283 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3775 and is usually paired with RFC 4285.

sections.title: Why Another Identifier Is Needed
sections.content:
The base Mobile IPv6 specification (RFC 3775) identifies mobility entities using an IPv6 address. RFC 4283 argues that it is essential to also identify them by other identifiers, for example a Network Access Identifier (NAI), an International Mobile Station Identifier (IMSI), or an application or deployment specific opaque identifier.

The RFC lists three things this makes possible: authentication and authorization using an existing AAA infrastructure or an HLR/AuC, dynamic allocation of a mobility anchor point, and dynamic allocation of a home address.

The option SHOULD be used when IKE/IPsec is not used to protect binding updates or binding acknowledgements. It is typically used together with the authentication option (RFC 4285), but it may be used on its own, for example to support accounting and billing.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes your address is not enough to say who you are. Like at school, the teacher wants your name, not just your seat number.

sections.title: The Mobile Node Identifier Option
sections.content:
The Mobile Node Identifier option is a new optional data field carried in Mobile IPv6 messages that include the Mobility header. It has four parts: Option Type, Option Length, Subtype and Identifier.

The option type, called MN-ID-OPTION-TYPE, has been assigned the value 8 by IANA and is an 8-bit field. The option length is an 8-bit unsigned integer counting the octets of the Subtype and Identifier fields. The Subtype says what kind of identifier is in the variable length Identifier field. The option does not have any alignment requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small label with four boxes: what kind of label it is, how long it is, what kind of name it carries, and the name itself.

sections.title: The MN-NAI Subtype
sections.content:
The MN-NAI mobility option uses the general format above with subtype value 1. It identifies the mobile node with an identifier of the form user@realm, as defined for the Network Access Identifier in RFC 4282.

Entities that implement this specification MUST implement the MN-NAI option. The RFC expects that other identifier types will be defined for the option in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Subtype 1 means the name is written like an email address, such as a username, an at sign and the place it belongs to.

sections.title: Where the Option Goes in a Message
sections.content:
There is one processing rule. When the Mobile Node Identifier option is present in a message containing a Mobility header, it MUST appear before any authentication-related option.

The reasoning is not spelled out in the RFC, but the rule fits its main use: the identifier says who is asking, and the authentication option that follows is then checked for that identity.
sections.plainLanguage: Say your name first, then show your proof. The name tag must come before the ID card.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 already has one way to identify nodes, the Home Address option, so the new option's vulnerabilities are similar to existing ones. The main concern is privacy: a permanent, stable identifier may make it possible to track a particular device or user as it moves between locations.

The MN-NAI reveals the home affiliation of a user. This may help an attacker identify the user, target specific victims, or probe the username space.

The RFC suggests three ways to reduce this: encrypting traffic at the link layer (which does not help against attackers elsewhere on the path to the home agent), encrypting the whole packet with IPsec as in RFC 3776, or using an authentication mechanism that allows privacy NAIs or temporary pseudonyms.

The RFC also notes that the identifier is only needed on the first registration at the home agent, and later registrations can use the home address. That shrinks the window of privacy exposure compared with RFC 3775.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tag that never changes lets a stranger follow you around. You can hide it, cover it up, or wear a nickname that changes.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
New mobility options must be assigned from the Mobile IPv6 numbering space. IANA has assigned the value 8 to MN-ID-OPTION-TYPE.

IANA also created a new namespace for the Subtype field. The only allocated value is the NAI, defined in RFC 4282. New values can be allocated using Standards Action (RFC 2434).
sections.plainLanguage: A keeper of the list gave this label the number 8 and started a list of name kinds, where only the username kind is on it so far.
